library.name: Process Hollowing & Cobalt Strike Beacon Loader
library.shortSubtitle: Malware Analysis · svchost.exe Memory Unmapping & PE Injection
library.overview: Imagine an intruder who wants to enter a high-security bank without raising an alarm. Instead of breaking down the front door in a ski mask, they hire an official armored bank truck, freeze it inside the garage before the driver even starts the route, and pocket two golden master keys: the first master key unlocks the rear cargo doors so they can empty all the legal bank gold and load their own covert crew inside, and the second master key unlocks the driver cab so they can reprogram the GPS route and release the brake. When the truck rolls out, every security camera and guard at the gate still sees the bank’s own trusted license plate and uniform. In this scenario (T1055.012, Process Hollowing & Cobalt Strike Beacon Loader) on WKS-04 (10.10.4), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: launching a Legitimate Windows Process, then hollowing Out the Original svchost.exe Code, then allocating Writable-Executable Memory, then hijacking the CPU Thread Context. Steps #1–#5 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Launching a Legitimate Windows Process, then Hollowing Out the Original svchost.exe Code, then Allocating Writable-Executable Memory, then Hijacking the CPU Thread Context, then Outbound HTTPS Command-and-Control Beacon. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

library.name: Fileless AMSI Memory Bypass & Reflective DLL Injection
library.shortSubtitle: Malware Analysis · amsi.dll 6-Byte Patch & In-Memory CLR Load
library.overview: Picture a glass-walled precision workshop that has its own automated X-Ray inspection belt built right inside the room, wired up to an elevated security watchtower overhead. Normally, whenever a red contraband canister slides onto the belt, the X-Ray scanner triggers a loud siren and slams a heavy steel drop-gate shut. Because the scanner circuit panel sits inside the exact same room as the workbench, a covert technician simply walks over, unbolts the blue glass safety hatch with a brass master wrench, pulls out all six copper inspection fuses, snaps in a single six-pin brass short-circuit jumper that cuts off the watchtower cable, and shuts the glass hatch again. Then, without ever unlocking the warehouse floor door or tipping the digital floor scale past zero kilograms, an overhead pneumatic air-tube drops floating parts onto a mid-air levitation ring where they snap together into a live hovering drone while the watchtower upstairs still reads all clear. In this scenario (T1562.001 and T1620, Fileless AMSI Memory Bypass & Reflective DLL Injection) on WKS-FIN-09, a hidden PowerShell session spawned by Microsoft Word sabotages its own in-process Antimalware Scan Interface before loading a stage-2 payload strictly in volatile RAM. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: locating the live scanner function in process memory, unlocking its read-only code page, overwriting six opening instruction bytes so every future scan returns an immediate skip result, and finally streaming a reflective assembly straight from HTTPS into unbacked RAM with zero disk writes. Steps #1-#4 walk that complete kill chain end-to-end, while Memory Forensics compares live patched pages and unbacked executable RAM against the clean disk. Primary detection correlates PowerShell Script Block Event ID 4104 with kernel memory-protection telemetry and empty-path CLR assembly load events.
